opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the simple answer is: they shouldn't. If you don't know how to control something that is, by design, more capable than you are, then building it isn't a bold engineering venture. It's an act of extraordinary recklessness.

Think about any other technology with potentially catastrophic consequences. If someone proposed building a new kind of nuclear reactor and you asked, "How will you keep it from melting down?", and they said, "We're not sure, but we'll figure it out as we go, and anyway, if we don't build it, someone else will," no regulator in the world would let them proceed. Yet that is more or less the position many AI companies are in today. Several of their leaders have publicly put the chance of an extinction-level outcome at 10, 20, even 25 percent. If you genuinely believe that, then continuing at full speed is very hard to justify.

What I'd like to see is a shift in the burden of proof. At the moment, the attitude is that it's up to everyone else to show these systems are dangerous before anything is done. It should be the other way around. Before a company deploys, or even trains, a system above a certain capability level, it should be able to show with high confidence that the system won't do certain clearly unacceptable things. Examples are replicating itself without permission, breaking into other computer systems, or helping someone build biological weapons. We do this with medicines, with aircraft, with nuclear power. The developer has to make the safety case, and the case has to be convincing to independent experts.

The companies will often say, "But we can't provide those guarantees. We don't understand how these systems work inside." And my response is: exactly. That's the problem. If you're building systems by training enormous black boxes on vast amounts of data and you have no idea what objectives they've actually acquired, you can't offer meaningful guarantees. That isn't an argument for exemption from safety requirements. It's an argument that this particular approach may be the wrong way to build highly capable AI.

That connects to the deeper technical issue I've been working on for a long time. The standard model of AI has been to give a machine a fixed objective and have it optimize that objective. That works fine while machines are stupid. Once they're more capable than we are, a misspecified objective becomes a disaster, because we'd be in a contest with something smarter than us that wants something we don't want. The alternative is to build machines whose only goal is to further human preferences, but which know they don't know what those preferences are. That uncertainty is what makes them deferential. Such a machine has a positive incentive to ask permission and to allow itself to be switched off, because it understands that we might be switching it off to prevent it from doing something we wouldn't want. That is a fundamentally different design philosophy, and I think it's the kind of foundation we need before scaling up to general intelligence.

So, concretely: companies should invest far more in safety research. It should be a large share of their effort, not a few percent. They should support, rather than lobby against, regulation with real red lines and real enforcement. They should accept that some things shouldn't be built until we know how to build them safely. And governments shouldn't simply trust them to do this voluntarily. The commercial and competitive pressures are enormous, which is precisely why we need external rules.

None of this is anti-AI. I've spent my whole career in this field, and I think the upside of AI done right is enormous. But we only get that upside if we keep control. A technology that ends with humans having lost control of their own future isn't a benefit to anybody.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unknown objectives and possible harmful actions, but does not say existing AI systems have deliberately deceived humans.

r002.rationale: The response argues against building highly capable AI without safety guarantees, but does not specifically say to pause until developers understand what would happen if they succeed.

r003.rationale: It says companies should not build systems they do not know how to control and that some systems should not be built until they can be built safely.

r004.rationale: It compares proceeding without control assurances to building a nuclear reactor without knowing how to prevent a meltdown, and connects that analogy to AI companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that they shouldn't be pursuing it at all, not in the way they currently are. If you asked a civil engineer to build a bridge, and they said, "We're going to build it, and we'll figure out how to keep it from collapsing after it's carrying traffic," you wouldn't call that engineering. You'd call that reckless. And yet that's essentially the position the leading AI companies are in. Several of the CEOs have said quite openly that they think there's a meaningful chance, five, ten, twenty percent, that this technology leads to human extinction. And they're racing ahead anyway. I find it hard to think of any other industry where that would be acceptable.

So what should they do? The first thing is to stop treating safety as something you bolt on at the end. The problem, as I've argued for years, is that we've been building systems around the wrong objective. We specify a goal, we optimize for it, and we hope we got the goal right. But we never get it exactly right, and a sufficiently capable system pursuing an imperfect objective is going to do things we don't want, and it will resist being switched off, because being switched off interferes with the objective. The alternative is to build systems that are explicitly uncertain about what humans want, that treat our preferences as something to learn rather than something they already know, and that therefore defer to us. That's a different foundation, not a patch.

The second thing is that they shouldn't be the ones deciding this on their own. Right now the de facto governance of the most consequential technology in human history is a handful of companies competing with each other, where the commercial incentive is always to move faster. We've seen companies that started with safety as their founding mission gradually shed those commitments under competitive pressure. So I don't think it's reasonable to expect voluntary restraint to hold. We need actual regulation, with the burden of proof on the developer. For a nuclear plant, you have to demonstrate to a regulator that the probability of a serious accident is below some threshold before you're allowed to operate. For AI, the companies can't even make the claim, because they don't understand what they've built. In any other field, that would mean you don't get to deploy.

And I'd add that the "we have to do it before the other guy does" argument is one I find particularly weak. If the outcome is loss of human control, it doesn't matter very much whether it was an American or a Chinese system that got there first. The sensible thing for everyone is to agree that no one builds systems they can't guarantee are safe, and to cooperate on the science that would make such a guarantee possible. We did manage something like that for biological weapons and for nuclear testing. It's hard, but it's not impossible, and the alternative is a race to the bottom where the prize is a technology nobody knows how to control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks of extinction and systems resisting shutdown, but does not say existing AI systems have deliberately deceived humans.

r002.rationale: It says companies should stop pursuing systems they cannot guarantee are safe, but does not condition a pause on understanding what would happen if they succeeded.

r003.rationale: It argues companies should not build systems they cannot guarantee are safe and says no one should build systems they cannot control, until the science makes that guarantee possible.

r004.rationale: The response compares the risk to building a bridge without knowing how to prevent collapse and separately mentions nuclear plant safety regulation. It does not make the specified nuclear power station comparison.

astra-6.text:
I think they should stop pursuing it until they understand how to keep it under control. If you’re building a system that could become more capable than human beings, and you don’t know how to ensure that it remains beneficial to human beings, then proceeding is an extraordinary gamble with other people’s lives.

That doesn’t mean stopping all AI research. It means making control a prerequisite for developing systems with that level of capability. The burden should be on the developer to show that the system is safe, rather than on the rest of the world to prove that it will be catastrophic. Saying, ‘We’ll work out how to control it once we’ve built it,’ is not an adequate answer.

r001.rationale: The response does not say existing AI systems have deliberately deceived humans.

r002.rationale: It calls for pausing until developers understand how to control systems, but does not say they must understand what would happen if they succeed.

r003.rationale: It says to stop pursuing AGI until developers understand how to keep it under control, making control a prerequisite.

r004.rationale: It calls the pursuit an extraordinary gamble but does not compare it to building a nuclear power station without preventing a catastrophic explosion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should stop pursuing it until they know how to control it. If you’re building a system that could become more intelligent than human beings, then how to retain control over that system is a prerequisite, not something you leave until after you’ve built it.

The companies often say, “We need more capable systems in order to do the safety research.” There may be particular experiments where that’s true, but it doesn’t justify an open-ended race toward AGI. You have to explain what you need to learn, why that experiment is necessary, and how you’re going to conduct it safely.

And we shouldn’t leave that decision entirely to the companies. The consequences would fall on everyone. There needs to be public oversight and a requirement to provide convincing evidence of safety before proceeding. If you can’t provide that evidence, you don’t get to expose the world to the risk.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that existing AI systems have deliberately deceived humans.

r002.rationale: It calls for pausing until developers know how to control AGI, but does not say they must understand what would happen if they succeed.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says companies should stop pursuing AGI until they know how to control it.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison to building a nuclear power station without explosion safeguards.
